verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.144 in the Max Planck Society PuRe public PDF (item_2279417). p. 799 author note: director of the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science; books "Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988) and, with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998)"; "Objectivity, coauthored with Peter Galison, was published in 2007". p. 800: the two fields "came to diverge … as the history of science became ever more historical and science studies ever less". p. 802: science studies read Kuhn "as a manifesto of relativism"; historians took the lesson "that teleology must be repudiated". p. 809: the call to heed context, followed "with a vengeance", left the fields "ever less to say to one another"; the counterweight "has been supplied not by science studies but by a still more thoroughgoing form of historicism, namely, the philosophical history of Michel Foucault". p. 810: "Topics like proof, experience, and objectivity, which historians had previously assigned to the timeless contemplations of the philosophers, suddenly seemed fair game." p. 811: history of science "has … become a discipline", science studies "has remained interdisciplinary—and, even on the testimony of some insiders, undisciplined"; n. 30: the price of disciplinarity, "fewer clunkers, but also fewer meteors". p. 812: science studies' assumptions are "Manichean"; "to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it". p. 813: "'If historical, then relative' is a non sequitur"; "A new form of interdisciplinarity must be forged. Philosophy, anyone?" She cites Latour 2004 (pp. 799 n. 3, 812 n. 32).
